items.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995
items.q: and we got together and I joined Basie.

ctx.x: Oh well that started years ago when I was in high school. My teacher, Henry L. Grant, who was also Duke Ellington’s teacher and Billy Taylor, Dr. Billy Taylor and I studied with him. And he was the orchestra teacher you know. And he gave me a flute to take home you know. So I took it home and after fooling with it a while I realized that I couldn’t do it without a teacher, you know. And at the time, you know I couldn’t afford a teacher and there wasn’t one available that I knew of. So I said I’ll just let it rest…

was looking for a tenor player you know, so he kept calling and calling. He called for a couple of years and I told him I was doing something, you know, and I couldn’t leave right then. So he just kept calling. Periodically he would call. And in the meantime I got a degree, a bachelor’s degree in flute, and we got together and I joined Basie. Well the thing was at the time I mean, what made me go with him because actually I had quit the road five years before I joined Basie. You know I’d given up on the road…
What was the audience response like? Did they like it?

items.title: Frank Wess — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: when I was with Basie, he might call a set and he’d play two tunes and he’d change it right there

ctx.x: Do you try to establish, you know, a connection with your audience or an intimacy?

Well, you know, that’s what this music is—communication. You can play anything you want as long as you don’t go off and leave the audience. You have to take them with you all the way. That’s one thing that you learn, and you can tell by the reaction of the audience, what’s going on. Just like, when I was with Basie, he might call a set and he’d play two tunes and he’d change it right there because he can tell by the reaction of the audience that it’s not what he should do right then. The thing is, you know your…
Yeah, I’m sure. You referenced Basie and how he measured what was going on in his audience. I remember you saying that you sat next to him. So, you tended to have the inside story.
